about: Labelled passages for reading prose into suggested changes (EXT-008). Original text written for these tests. 'entries' is the story bible before reading; each case's 'expected' lists what a careful reader would suggest, each item with the kind of reading it needs: name (the entry's name), alias (one of its other names), pronoun (only 'he' or 'she' says who), epithet (a description, given as a guess for the author), new_entry (someone the bible lacks), narration (the narrator says it, so it is a fact), speech (a character says it: a belief, never a fact), disclosure (one character tells another). 'not_facts' are things the passage must not make facts: what is only said, and what is only near the truth. 'recorded' is an answer written by hand to look like a model's, including typical mistakes, and replayed by the scripted model in CI; '@key' stands for an entry's id.

cases.text:
Wren Halloway came in out of the rain at the Ferry House and shook the water from her hood. Ada was already behind the counter, counting coppers into a tin. The keeper of the house slid the tide ledger across without a word.

A stranger in a grey coat sat by the fire, turning his hat in his hands. He gave his name as Corin Vale and said he had come for the crossing.

entities.name: Corin Vale

cases.text:
“Osric Pell is one of the Tidewardens,” Ada Quill said, low, so the men at the fire would not hear. “He swore the oath at midwinter.”

Wren shook her head and went on mending the net. Outside, Bram Tolley, who had worn the Tidewardens’ grey since he was a boy, stamped the snow from his boots.

cases.text:
Osric Pell climbed to the lamp room of Marrow Light at dusk. He had kept the brass sextant in a drawer beneath the lens for thirty winters, wrapped in oilcloth against the salt. The old keeper did not trust the mainland instruments.

Below him, the girl who poled the ferry tied up at the jetty; she had brought the oil, as she did every week.

references: the girl who poled the ferry

cases.text:
That night Ada Quill told Wren Halloway the truth: Osric Pell was her brother, and had been since before either of them could walk. Wren believed her at once; it explained the way Ada watched the light.

Ada owned the tide ledger, and she pressed it into Wren’s hands, but only to hold until morning.

facts.quote: she pressed it into Wren’s hands
